We introduce a $p$-divisibility concept for the Fourier coefficients of Siegel modular functions and p-adic linear independence conjectures for their coefficients. The first major result shows the $p$-divisibility properties of the $p$-adically modified Siegel gamma factors align with the $p$-divisibility concept for Siegel modular functions. The second result validates the $p$-divisibility conjecture for the canonical Siegel theta function, and we also provide new insights into the $p$-divisibility of the Fourier coefficients of Siegel theta functions based on the $p$-adic properties of Gaussian integers.

We introduce a notion of precise sequence within the context of the rigid fibrations $\mathcal{F}_n$, an infinite sequence of formal fibrations representing the $n$-th nilpotent quotient of a free group, and establish the key property of rigidity in precise sequences. The primary tools employed in the proof involve the theories of groups and formal groups, as well as the techniques of translation and the explicit structure of the fibers in the rigid fibrations $\mathcal{F}_n$, established in the prior work \cite{MR3124728}.

The concept of specific heat being defined as the expectation value of the energy fluctuation within a system under a canonical ensemble forms the basis of a statistical mechanical model. This model utilizes the energy density of 2D grid systems, known as Pauli lattices. The model focuses on specific heat, denoted as $\widetilde{C}_V$, in relation to the energy fluctuation of two-spin Hamiltonians in 2D Pauli lattices. The potential physical significance of this model is significantly greater than initially assumed due to the diverse properties exhibited by these Hamiltonians.

This study presents Zeroing Neural Networks, an adaptable and efficient approach to solving matrix problems with time-varying parameters. Traditional methods like singular value decomposition and power iteration struggle with these dynamic problems. NZNN, however, leverages a ZNN matrix calculator to overcome these limitations and effectively tackle problems with time-varying constraints. It offers adaptability and reliability, making it a robust tool for handling complex matrix problems in dynamic environments.

This study introduces a novel computational model of sensory fields, incorporating on-off center-surround sensitivity patterns derived from a biological mechanism that adjusts sensitivity based on local mean intensity. These dynamic sensitivity patterns are used to extract on-off center-surround sensory fields, which are then used to process and classify the MNIST dataset. A modified LeNet architecture, integrating these sensory fields as input, is evaluated and compared to a baseline LeNet using both standard and corrupted datasets. Experimental results indicate that the proposed network achieves superior accuracy under various noise conditions and enhanced robustness when contrasted with the baseline model.

Future large-scale X-ray missions will likely employ wide-field instruments. The development of such equipment necessitates the creation of novel or repurposed methods for designing X-ray optical systems. Current techniques for creating wide-field X-ray optics involve incorporating field-dependent corrections into the surface shape of the optic, allowing computer-controlled polishing techniques to manufacture these correctors. Several approaches to this concept have been explored. The paper will examine the current state of these methods, focusing on three key correction methods: dual-grating, double curvature, and double tilt. It will also highlight the benefits and constraints of each approach, with a specific example being the potential integration of these correctors into the XRISM X-IFU detector to achieve its full field of view.

The core principle of Bloch's theorem in non-uniform graphene sheets is its violation when a specific magnetic twist angle of $2\pi$ is present. This occurs because the essential su(2) symmetry of the magnetic translation group becomes realized in a projective form under such twist angles. Utilizing a magnetic twist angle of $2\pi$ during stacked graphene layers results in remarkable electronic properties due to enhanced symmetry. Specifically, it leads to the emergence of reentrant flat bands at zero energy and electronic orbitals with vanishing angular momentum. Moreover, the interlayer coupling strength significantly influences the critical twist angles leading to these remarkable properties, ultimately allowing for precise predictions of higher-twist angle moire systems.

This research introduces an enhanced LSTM model that enables the development of a more robust steganographic system, capable of concealing secret messages within seemingly ordinary text, which can then be decoded using the appropriate key. The initial framework utilized Chinese character frequency distributions, crafted specifically for crafting steganographic content tailored to a specific target language, which was decoded utilizing a simplified form of the XOR algorithm. By integrating the initial layer of the LSTM network, the capacity to improve overall system security, measured through both its resilience against the Steghunter tool and its resilience against manual inspection, was achieved, which resulted in a significant improvement in security and also increased the length of the secret message that could be embedded.

High-voltage direct current transmission systems play a vital role in integrating renewable energy and ensuring power grid stability. Optimizing their operation is crucial for minimizing costs, and researchers have been exploring the use of deep reinforcement learning for this purpose. However, previous approaches failed to leverage invaluable insights from system operators, specifically, expertise in predicting high-voltage direct current transmission unit commitments. This paper proposes incorporating this expertise into deep reinforcement learning algorithms via cost model learning, enabling agents to leverage cost models to derive detailed, interpretable insights into operator decision-making and, ultimately, improve the agents' performances. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding up to 10.5% tighter lower bounds and a 14.3% significant reduction in computational time compared to existing deep reinforcement learning methods.

The material, $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, displays a variety of complex magnetic phenomena such as non-trivial three-dimensional order, fractionalization, and the emergence of a three-state lattice model known as the Kitaev model. A recent investigation has delved into the material's magnetic and structural properties under high pressure using neutron diffraction and high-frequency EPR spectroscopy. Results have shown that an unusual magnetic phase transition occurs at approximately 3 GPa above which a three-magnon resonance splits. This indicates a collapse of the previously reported three-state Kitaev antiferromagnetic state which was stable below 2 GPa. As pressure continues to increase, a new magnetic phase emerges characterized by an in-plane periodicity of two units, aligned with the material's natural tendency to form pairs of coupled magnetic ions, known as dimers. This observation is also confirmed by the material's EPR properties, which indicate a substantial decrease in the complex spin-orbit interaction responsible for its magnetic properties, dropping to less than 1 meV. A new magnetic phase emerges at approximately 9.5 GPa characterized by an unusual magnetic ordering and is believed to be a highly short-range state in which neighboring spins are locked in a rigid, parallel configuration. A theoretical framework has been developed to explain these results and to identify the specific type of magnetic ordering observed in this material, which is consistent with a predicted type-K state in which neighboring spins are locked in a rigid, parallel

This research proposes a novel causal inference approach, a causal framework involving treated and nearby control units. It is argued that when a synthetic controls estimator achieves consistency, it essentially estimates a theory-based model under certain conditions. This theory-based model incorporates data solely from the control group observed before treatment occurs. It is shown through formal proofs and real-world case studies, including COVID-19 data, that T-NECI outperforms synthetic controls by offering superior point estimates, more reliable uncertainty quantification, and improved out-of-sample predictive performance. The reliability of T-NECI was verified using COVID-19 testing data for accurate inference on treated and new units. The proposed approach is made available for download on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/achoudhary/T-NECI.

Graphs that represent complex data can have diverse topological structures. The application of Gaussian Kernels in topological graphs restricts their usability to graphs with the same node and edge connections. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Gaussian Wasserstein Distance that incorporates the Gromov-Hovnikov Distance, enabling the comparison of graphs with varying topologies. This distance is computed in real-time on both the edge and node locations. To protect user privacy, we introduce a novel system for local differential privacy, allowing both users and server to be protected. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated in the classification of brain connectivity graphs with Alzheimer's-related abnormalities.

The role of plasma interactions with high-intensity lasers is gaining prominence for developing compact particle accelerators. The laser filament technique, characterized by self-steepling of the pulse front, offers a way to manage electron injection and acceleration through a controllable process. By utilizing a two-dimensional full relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell plasma simulation with an implicit scheme, we investigated how different polarization states affect electron injection and acceleration when interacting with a plasma under specific conditions. Our findings reveal that when a linearly polarized laser enters the plasma, we observe the creation of a localized over-density, time-varying electric fields, and cavity formation. The behavior of these structures is influenced by the polarization state of the laser, which also controls electron injection into the plasma. Moreover, we discovered that only when a circularly polarized laser enters the plasma, we observe the development of shock waves and wakefields, characterized by cavities with transverse gradients in the electric field. This enables us to study electron injection into the plasma and identify two distinct injection mechanisms depending on the polarization state. The linearly polarized case yields a single beam with multi-peaked energy spectrum and angular distribution, while the circularly polarized case yields a beam with single peak energy, angle, and energy spread distributions.

A platinum sample with high purity was used to set new constraints on various areas including double beta decay, nuclear matrix elements, dark matter detection through induced reactions and neutrinoless double beta decay.  By utilizing the gamma-ray spectrum from the platinum sample along with simulations from a quantum molecular dynamics model, researchers found that the double beta decay width for $^{194}$Pt to $^{194}$Pd lies within the 0.5-10 s$^{-2}$ range, leading to further estimation of nuclear matrix elements.  In addition, the study set stringent limits on dark matter induced processes through platinum-nickel transitions and platinum-rhodium transitions, specifically under the assumption of neutrino non-oscillation.  By comparing the study's findings with other constraints, it was observed that the current research sets more restrictive limits on certain parameters.

We investigate the dimensional regularization renormalization of the flavor-singlet axial-vector current.  The effect of the axial anomaly on the renormalization group is considered.  The Wilson coefficient of the anomaly operator in the axial-vector two-point function is analyzed.  The contributions from the gluon field-strength anomaly and the gluino field-strength anomaly to the axial-vector two-point function are computed at ${\cal O}(\alpha_s)$ and the QCD result is generalized to a dimension-$D$ Majorana super-Yang-Mills theory.  The Wilson coefficient's impact on the axial-vector renormalization constant $Z_\eta$ is discussed.  The axial-vector current $j_\mu^5$ is expressed as a linear combination of two basis operators $T_1^\mu$ and $T_2^\mu$, with the renormalization-group eigenvalues $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ and their associated running-coupling couplings $A_1$ and $A_2$ determined.

Image color consistency is a pressing issue in vision tasks, particularly when dealing with multiple cameras, due to variations in color perception and technical factors. A simple yet effective solution could be deep image tinting to correct color discrepancies, but current techniques often lack robustness. This proposal introduces a novel method for cross-camera deep image color alignment using an auto-encoding approach. This method employs two auto-encoders, which cross-decode each other's output, minimizing cross-camera color differences while preserving the original image's hue through the application of perceptual loss. A key aspect of this approach involves leveraging a color space tailored for human perception, specifically the CIELAB space, to facilitate cross-camera color alignment. A further enhancement is achieved by training the model with a combination of RGB and HSV color representations, which provides a richer color depth. This method achieved exceptional results with an average PSNR score of 31.46dB on the PASCAL VOC dataset, surpassing existing techniques by 0.94dB. A proposed application of this approach is demonstrated in an efficient multi-view object detection system, showcasing its effectiveness.

Recent studies on the three-dimensional generalized Ermakov system have been limited and poorly understood by dark matter in the arXiv. Our focus is on expanding the scope to the $n$-dimensional system with general nonlinearities and applying the method of inverse mapping to classify its Lie symmetries. We discover two new conservation laws using Noether's method, corresponding to previously identified symmetry generators, and verify them through direct calculation. The application of the separation of variables technique to the resulting non-stretch Hamiltonian yields a novel set of conservation laws. Our work establishes the Lie symmetries for the $n$-dimensional generalized Ermakov system for the first time and provides the complete equations of motion for the separated quantities.

This research outlines a new method for a transit vehicle to automatically acquire its schedule information via a ubiquitous wireless network. The system's effectiveness relies on using recurrent neural networks to decode the vehicle's schedule information, or transit feed, from a complex format known as General Purpose Schedule. A model was created to generate the new, unachievable format and test subjects, including both recurrent and feed-forward neural networks, were able to produce schedule information comparable to that produced by a designated software decoder. However, due to size constraints, feed-forward networks exhibited an average of 12% more location estimation error than recurrent networks, whose performance matched that of the designated decoder.

This study explores the concept of learning prototype functions categorized in latent spaces. In doing so, it addresses the issue of intra-class variability prevalent in few-shot learning algorithms. In contrast to existing intra-class prototypes, which are typically generated within the feature space using averaging techniques, the proposed approach seeks to construct representatives for each cluster within the latent space. This allows for the creation of an optimization objective that identifies an optimal clustering in the latent space and its corresponding prototype. In few-shot learning scenarios, these prototypes can effectively minimize the loss function. In an ideal situation, the clustering objective and the subsequent formation of prototypes can accurately represent the underlying data distribution. In order to achieve effective data distribution clustering, the study presents two algorithms: a clustering method that utilizes a pre-trained model and an optimization technique that incrementally refines the clustering. In conjunction with few-shot learning objectives, the performance of these algorithms is evaluated on benchmark datasets for both few-shot image classification and few-shot relation extraction. Empirical results demonstrate the competitiveness of these algorithms with state-of-the-art methods.

A novel form of non-invertible (charge) symmetry known as persistent symmetry presents an interesting possibility in both non-relativistic and relativistic systems. These symmetries comprise a non-abelian collection, featuring a unique non-invertible element denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, under which a system remains unchanged. The persistent symmetry class arises from a more comprehensive symmetry in higher dimensions, known as a non-invertible symmetry preserving an interface. Through a theoretical analysis, we demonstrate how a theorem can be formulated to connect a $(d+1)$-dimensional persistent symmetry preserving an interface with a $d$-dimensional theory containing a conserved current that cannot be derived from any anomaly.

A graph is considered semi-transitive if it has more than four vertices and any three vertices with connected edges form a connected path. Researchers have shown that the maximal semi-transitive graphs in a class where every vertex can be reached by an even number of edges from any other, are either complete or form a specific pattern of connections. Further, they found that these graphs contain specific types of connections and their underlying structure can be described in a particular way. In addition, they proved that these graphs can be ordered in a specific way, with certain types of connections forming a specific pattern of connections. Finally, they found that these graphs can be ordered in a way that their underlying structure can be described in a particular way, with certain types of connections forming a specific pattern of connections.

A novel approach utilizing deep neural networks has been explored for detecting hadronic tau particles based on information collected from the CMS main calorimeter.  The deep neural network model, specifically looking at simplified CMS phase I upgrade data, has been successfully tested with significant improvements in detection efficiency, achieving a 0.787 efficiency at 50% background rejection, while also showing potential for particle study.

The coming Big Data era, exemplified by the Rubin Science Project, will generate immense data sets from upcoming surveys like the LSST, leading to a pressing need for efficient data classification techniques. We investigated the effectiveness of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in handling large data sets and categorization tasks, specifically testing their potential in the context of LSST data and galaxy properties. Through our study, we found that BNNs achieved comparable results to conventional Neural Networks for a specific small sample, but struggled to maintain their performance with data drawn from the LSST survey. This limitation stems partly from BNN's training data limitations, partly from over-optimistic assumptions about generalization. We found ways to improve the accuracy of BNNs by utilizing training data from a standard data set and employing a transfer learning method, thereby achieving better results. This study highlights the challenges in applying BNNs to large data sets and suggests that, with careful handling, they could play a significant role in the coming Big Data era.

Our investigation focuses on the impact of vector properties on large-mode area photonic lattice fibers, specifically examining intermodal linear coupling to modal intermodal nonlinearity within these fibers. To achieve this, we developed a set of simplified equations, which, despite their reduced complexity, capture the intricate interplay between vector properties and modal coupling. The application of these simplified equations to two distinct types of photonic lattice fibers, designated as PL1 and PL2, allowed us to explore intermodal non-linear phenomena, particularly Bragg resonance and four-wave mixing. Moreover, our research highlights the interdependence of intermodal nonlinearity, Bragg resonance, and effective area in large-mode area photonic lattice fibers, which can facilitate the integration of non-linear effects into such fibers, thereby enhancing their performance.

Our research is based on a generalization of the fundamental theorem associated with the B-type Coxeter group, which is built upon a monoid structure composed of specific compositions and extensions of these operations. This composition and extension framework results in the construction of a monoid that can be applied to any set. Notably, when applied to a two-element set, this constructed monoid corresponds to the well-known symmetric monoid of the fourth order, also referred to as the symmetric group or permutation group. Furthermore, this construction provides novel insights and methods for calculating the statistics of T. Brenti's generalized descent set, thereby offering new perspectives and approaches in this area of study.

Two related knapsack problem variations, the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, have been the subject of research due to their practical applications in areas such as data mining and network design. The former involves selecting sets of items to maximize profit while respecting a shared resource constraint, effectively combining the features of both the Knapsack Problem and the Partition Problem. The BMC Problem, on the other hand, seeks to identify a set of subsets within given constraints that yield the highest total coverage. In this research, the development of local search algorithms for a novel encoding of these problems is presented. By utilizing a representation that enables the local search to access the set property, the authors demonstrate its ability to recognize shared used items and uncover the problem's underlying mathematical structure. Moreover, the authors propose a novel swapping algorithm that operates on this set-based encoding and achieves a polynomial time complexity. Experimental evaluations using extensive testing and comparisons with the existing literature reveal the effectiveness of these local search algorithms in solving both BMC and SKP instances, showcasing their ability to produce high-quality solutions within a short timeframe.

A major operator in SLOVENIA has approached us to predict customer behavior in online gaming, specifically whether they will make a deposit within a 3-month period. To tackle this challenge, we're using Machine Learning methods, starting with data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model creation. Our approach, demonstrated through a synthetic dataset, provides an in-depth explanation of the techniques used, aiming to facilitate adoption by industry professionals in online gaming. This work serves as a reference for implementing these strategies in real-world scenarios.

The study of the 2D Ising Field Theory under a magnetic field reveals a single non-self-adjoint Hamiltonian with a complex spectrum, featuring one essential singular eigenvalue at a specific magnetic field strength of $-i h_{critical}$. This eigenvalue's associated eigenfunction exhibits a link to the theory's unique Liouville solution, encompassing the critical point at which the theory transitions between two distinct phases.

We investigate lattice calculations of transversity and generalized parton distributions with large-momentum effective theory, including meson light-cone wave functions, twist-2 and twist-3 quark transversity and gluon distributions, and meson pseudotensor and quark tensor currents. Our results from lattice QCD and QCDmeson-LatticePT are combined, after proper renormalization and scale evolution, to extract transversity and gluon distributions at various momentum fractions $x$ and $t^2/\mu^2$. Our findings for transversity and gluon distributions show qualitative consistency with experimental data and extractions from global fits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the meson light-cone wave functions, and transversity and gluon distributions, exhibit correct behavior under scale evolution, and provide estimates for the flavor singlet and gluon contributions under scale evolution.

We investigate the light-by-light scattering process in heavy-ion collisions, which occurs in the context of electromagnetic interactions between virtual particles. We establish a model that accounts for the Coulomb phase space distortion. Our analysis reveals that the Coulomb distortion significantly affects the available phase space for light-by-light scattering events involving low-transverse-momentum leptons, particularly in cases where the light-like lepton trajectory deviates slightly from its original path. This model can be extended to other heavy-ion collision processes, such as electron-nucleus and positron-nucleus interactions, and even to electron-lead collisions, all of which can be described within the framework of the equivalent photon approximation. Furthermore, the implementation of the one-loop Coulomb distortion effect in these interactions is also discussed.

To enhance cyclist safety, there's a growing need for advanced safety systems that can evaluate road-cyclist interactions and provide comprehensive safety information. Current studies primarily concentrate on establishing effective safety systems for cyclists, yet they often neglect the crucial step of explaining road conditions to drivers in an understandable way. Our research proposes a novel approach to describing road risks for cyclists through a combination of factors including cyclist presence, road environment, and traffic patterns. By introducing context-aware risk indicators and utilizing video-based features, our method accurately predicts significant collisions between cyclists and vehicles in a real-world setting. Our experiments on two large-scale datasets reveal the superiority of our approach over existing methods, with a notable improvement in performance. Furthermore, our findings suggest that advanced safety systems for cyclists should be grounded in advanced data analysis techniques.

This paper proposes an innovative approach to ensure the safety and robustness of motion planning for dynamic robots in the presence of uncertain model parameters and sensor data. A key challenge in dynamic robot motion planning is that minor deviations can lead to cascading errors, making it difficult to account for the effects of uncertainty. To address this, we suggest a method based on Control Barrier Functions that incorporates uncertainty into motion planning. This method uses a Control Barrier Function to define a safe boundary, beyond which uncertainty is assumed not to affect the system. Our numerical results show that our approach significantly reduces collision risk and ensures system safety even when dealing with dynamic robots.

Given a ring $R$, under specific conditions, its center $Z$ enables a factorization of the enveloping ring $E(R)$ as $E(R) \cong R \otimes_{Z} R \cong R \otimes_{Z} R \otimes_{Z} \cdots \otimes_{Z} R \, (n \text{ times})$ for some integer $n \geq 2$. This property holds for all finite $p$-groups under certain conditions and more broadly applies to non-commutative Artin algebras with finite enveloping dimension. This research yields new insights into the nilpotence of ideals in Artin algebras, their abelianity constraints, and confirms the occurrence of Lagrange's Theorem for ideals in such algebras.

This study investigates the underlying mechanisms that allow deep neural networks to accurately classify inputs despite adversarial interference. Focusing on a basic two-layer convolutional network, we demonstrate that a particular transformation of its features is resilient to adversarial examples. Our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of this transformation in withstanding attacks is directly correlated to the presence of certain frequencies in its feature maps, which are naturally generated in specific network layers. Moreover, we develop an enhancement technique that amplifies the influence of these critical layers on the network's output, achieving a level of robustness against various adversarial attacks, across diverse datasets and architectures, surpassing existing robustness-enhancement methods.

We approach singular limit and entropy-admissibility issues in nonlocal traffic models with a broad class of interaction functions in a systematic manner. We demonstrate in the first instance that the difference between nonlocal and local traffic models can be limited by an error term that shrinks as the nonlocality's support decreases, specifically at a rate of O(1/ln(1/δ)) given certain conditions, including first-order nonlocal models and periodic settings, or at a rate of O(δ^(α+2)/3) for second-order nonlocal models and torus settings. We also introduce a condition to ensure that admissible solutions of nonlocal models converge to admissible solutions of local models, as δ goes to zero. We derive an explicit entropy-inequality form for first-order nonlocal models and prove that solutions of both first-order and second-order models converge to the locally-conserved energy entropy solution of the relevant locally-conserved equation at rates of O(δ^(α+2)/3) and O(δ^(α+1)/2), respectively.

A complex surface known as a dilation surface can be thought of as a modified version of a complete flat surface with cone-like singularities, achieved through limits on regions of the complex plane given by polynomial structures. Previous studies found links within boundaries on compact surfaces that separate regions of zero area into distinct components and were shown to exist within the boundaries of certain types of dilation surfaces. In this study, we present a revised definition of dilation surfaces that generalizes the previous understanding. Utilizing the properties of zero-area loops within a generalized dilation surface, we establish the existence of a new class of links known as horizon saddle links, characterized by specific properties related to their limits and the behavior of tangent lines. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these horizon saddle links and the motion of geodesic rays on a modified version of a two-dimensional surface with a finite number of cone-like singularities. Our investigation reveals that as these geodesic rays approach their endpoints, they exhibit a linearity property in certain intervals, and we also establish a connection between these intervals and a previously studied class of links. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these horizon saddle links and the motion of unbounded geodesic rays on a modified version of a two-dimensional surface with a finite number of cone-like singularities, showing that each such ray originates from a point within the set of singularities and is parallel to a link within the set of horizon saddle links, while also proving the existence of links within the set of horizon saddle links

A human brain network is characterized through functional connections between brain regions, measured using brain imaging techniques. Building upon the network framework's ability to capture complex relationships, we employed total correlation estimation from information theory to construct a brain map. Analyzing 100 adolescent brains, we discovered a previously unexplored brain region network structure, characterized by two distinct communities and numerous connected pathways. Our study also highlights the benefits of a new TC estimation method that enables reliable high-dimensional data analysis. As an application of this new approach, we demonstrate the detection of brain area associations that were previously obscured by the application of a widely used but inadequate approach of relying on pairwise correlations between areas.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transform can be understood as a way to represent functions on R^n in terms of their values and derivatives at the origin, via a representation in terms of polynomials with complex coefficients in n variables. This concept has been extended to a more general case where functions with values in a Clifford algebra are considered, and it is proven that a similar Segal-Bargmann transform can be applied in this context.

We are focusing on a Gaussian field with a specified marginal distribution in our calculations. By deriving an expression for the pathwise conditioning Gaussian map's strong solution under the general setting of L2 space, we demonstrate its complete continuity. This allows us to obtain the density function representing the Gaussian field conditioned on specific values. Our techniques can be applied in scenarios such as fractional Brownian motion and Gaussian processes with kernels.

A military scenario is addressed where an enemy obstructs communication between an airborne sensor network and its ground-based counterpart by deploying a jamming drone, thus severing the link. To restore connectivity, a swarm of intelligent drones is deployed as adaptive bridges to restore the sensor network connection through wireless communication. The swarm's objective is to minimize energy consumption while ensuring the sensor network's linked status, requiring their movement to optimal positions as feedback from the drones is obtained. Utilizing an array of sensing drones, ground, and air stations, an algorithm was developed to identify the optimal drone paths ensuring network connection with minimal total length, resulting in a graph-to-tree mapping method that yields distance-optimal drone paths to safeguard the sensor network's link.

A future long-baseline neutrino experiment, DUNE, will significantly contribute to multiple breakthroughs in neutrino physics as it employs a massive detector, D0, located deep underground. By doing so, it will define neutrino oscillation parameters with unprecedented accuracy and aid in understanding the mass hierarchy of neutrinos. Moreover, it will enhance our knowledge of neutrino interactions and offer the capability to detect neutrinos emitted from supernovae explosions.

A novel, machine learning-based top tagging approach has been developed and presented.
The approach employs network models to enhance identification capabilities for top quark decays.
A unique method utilizing Shapley values quantifies the importance of individual events to the overall tagging performance.
Using top tags from high-luminosity LHC ttbar and WZ events processed with a simulated CMS infrastructure, the new top tags demonstrate excellent discrimination power with a significant 10-15% improvement over alternative top tagging performance without heavy network training.
The developed top tags exhibit robustness across various heavy particle decays, including third generation fermions, and are therefore suitable for multiple analysis contexts.

This document establishes a precise definition for Virtual Organizations, defined as collaborations between software agents working together to achieve their goals. We refine Virtual Organizations using formal methods, making them more specific and reducing flexibility. The document proves two key aspects: (a) any Virtual Organization can be transformed into one that follows a particular structure, and (b) collaborative organizations with goals that depend on multiple factors can be transformed into those with single-factor dependent goals.

A key component of model-free Reinforcement Learning, experience replay has been extensively utilized in model-based and model-free settings. This paper delves into experience replay's application in model-free policy optimization, specifically in non-linear function approximation. It reveals that the average of returns from randomly sampled trajectories significantly reduces variance compared to the running average of all seen trajectories, which is the standard approach. Following this discovery, variance dimention experience replay is introduced, leveraging all seen trajectory data while prioritizing recent experiences to minimize variance and exploit data correlations. Large-scale experiments across diverse environments demonstrate its efficacy, outperforming the standard replay baseline and other recent techniques on sample efficiency, particularly in model-free settings.

Recently, the superbosonization equation was proposed as a superintegral transform for deciding supermatrix models after integrating them over specific supercompact Lie groups with special superfunctions applied. This transformation is claimed to project these superfunctions onto representations aligned with the supermatrix group's irreducible components. We argue that this concept has significant overlaps with the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation previously described in mathematical physics literature.

This research introduces a novel learning framework for predicting future frames in video sequences, where accurate predictions are heavily dependent on understanding subtle motion details. Traditional methods often overlook these details, resulting in blurry predictions. To address this challenge, a detailed space-time learning approach is proposed, utilizing Motion Aspect Disentanglement to separate temporal representations based on distinct motion characteristics. A modular recurrent neural network architecture, MoDeRNN, is designed to model these characteristics individually, enabling the temporal module to effectively capture motion dynamics and generate high-quality predictions. Moreover, a disentanglement objective is introduced to accurately reflect real-world motion characteristics, leading to MoDeRNN's superior performance in various video prediction benchmarks.

In JavaScript, pointers are simplified to memory address ranges, known as references/wrappers. The garbage collector ensures all active references to a given object remain, preventing premature deletion. However, a garbage collector adds significant overhead, impacting performance. This is particularly problematic in performance-critical areas, such as native modules. 

This research introduces Josephine, a garbage-collecting module for Rust that leverages JavaScript's wrapper properties to inform the garbage collector. It can be utilized in native modules, significantly reducing the limitations associated with garbage collection.

This research investigates the relationship between observations at high-energy colliders and those of neutrinoless double-beta decay, under the assumption that neutrinos are a mixture of sterile and active states. Unlike previous studies, which mainly focused on production rates and masses of neutral particles, our analysis specifically explores how different active components contribute to neutrinoless double-beta decay. Furthermore, we examine the correlation between experimental results from high-energy colliders and neutrinoless double-beta decay across various scenarios of neutral masses and active components.

Achieving reliable communication at the channel's limit often requires long codewords and complex decoding methods, such as belief propagation with cycle breaking, which can be computationally expensive. A novel decoding strategy combines the benefits of belief propagation with the error-correcting capabilities of polar codes, offering better performance at a lower cost. By leveraging binary erasure channel polar codes, this strategy reduces the number of long codewords, thereby cutting decoding complexity, and maintains strong frame error rates even at low signal-to-noise ratios.

When merging astronomical images, their point spread functions need to be calculated by combining the individual images' PSFs in quadrature, which includes accounting for shot noise from co-added exposures and the variance in each individual exposure.

We utilize the concept of free energy to develop a theory of fracture in a crystal lattice. Our model incorporates two key factors - the surface energy representing fracture surface costs and the energy lost due to lattice displacement near crack edges. With this framework, we derive a fundamental equation describing the dynamic structure of a crack in a static plane strain state. Our analysis reveals that the strength of the crack is inherently linked to the strength of the material, with no independent weakness. The model's parameters can be obtained through simple experiments, providing us with the ability to predict the fracture surface energy based on measured elastic properties and fracture surface energy per unit area.

We establish a probabilistic connection between complex SLEs governed by random log-gases and the Gaussian free field within a bounded domain. This coupling is achieved under conditions of weak inflection by demonstrating that a certain joint density function corresponding to the SLEs paths coincides with the welding density function, a concept defined by the Gaussian free field's interpretation of the upper half-plane's boundary, resulting in the SLEs paths from the random log-gas model aligning with the Gaussian free field's welding paths.

In the case of Navier-Stokes equations with time-dependent external forces and periodic initial conditions, we derive explicit estimates of the maximum norm in terms of a given, positive, minimum norm by a selected, positive, and sufficiently large parameter. Moreover, under the condition that the initial data have a sufficiently small norm, we find explicit estimates of the maximum norm in terms of the minimum norm with a parameter. This result further generalizes the case where $\alpha\to\infty$, recovering the previously established explicit lower bounds in terms of the maximum norm in the case of zero initial data, as demonstrated in the work of Landau.

A significant issue in the context of "trust but verify" is the verification of quantum computation outcomes. Currently, the most efficient verification protocols rely on interactive or quantum-assisted methods, but they require substantial computational resources to be completed within linear time. In contrast, this study presents a non-interactive and traditional approach to verifying quantum computation. By employing error-correcting codes that are linear and allow for local testing, such as the Hadamard codes, the computation can be preceded by preprocessing that embeds the code into a larger circuit. As a result, traditional methods can now verify complex, polynomially-sized quantum operations with minimal resources, leveraging the commutative property of diagonal matrices.

A blockchain is a decentralized network ledger that records data across multiple nodes, ensuring data integrity and security. By adding a layer of transparency and control to the Internet of Things, blockchain technology can be applied to the tracking of goods within a supply chain context. This research paper focuses on applying blockchain technology to the tracking of goods within the food industry, where a smart contract is combined with a blockchain framework to monitor the condition of goods as they travel through the supply chain. To achieve this, a blockchain framework is proposed, incorporating an oracle that gathers sensor data and triggers the execution of a pre-agreed smart contract between parties involved in the transaction. This work demonstrates the utility of its blockchain framework through the development of a prototype system, which was evaluated and tested.

Representations of cell forms generated by traditional 2D or 3D geometric methods can facilitate research on understanding and predicting cell shape behavior, yet they have inherent resolution limits. In contrast, cell shape neural representations utilize high-dimensional continuous fields, potentially offering a more accurate form of geometric description. To further advance this area, our study develops implicit neural representations of cell shapes for generative modeling purposes. We achieve this by creating and comparing different neural networks that utilize cells in training sets, and also by employing larger datasets. We discovered that certain network architectures yield superior generative capabilities, and larger datasets can enhance model performance. Moreover, our implicit representations can be trained independently of 2D or 3D image data and can be used to predict new cell shapes based on features such as nuclear area and physical confinement. We anticipate that our methodology will contribute significantly to research focused on understanding and predicting cell shape behavior.

Blind individuals often face significant challenges in reading due to 
document image scanning errors, which can be addressed by leveraging 
the inherent table structure to convert images into editable text format.
Developing a table recognition system that generates human-readable HTML
code is a complex task, and our proposed solution, DOCNAV, leverages the
navigability of documents to enhance the readability of generated HTML code.
Our experiments conducted on three datasets reveal that DOCNAV significantly
outperforms its peer, TabNet, by producing more accurate HTML code and 
improved overall readability.

Pre-trained language models based on the Transformer architecture have revolutionized natural language processing, achieving state-of-the-art performance on numerous tasks. Despite their widespread success, recent studies examined two aspects of these models: their inherent self-attention recurrence and the effectiveness of next token prediction. We introduce XLPretransformer XLNet, a new pre-training approach that incorporates recurrence and next token prediction, and overcome previous limitations. Our XLNet model overcomes the drawbacks of previous BERT models by allowing any token to be predicted in any position within a given sequence, and thus achieves superior performance on numerous NLP tasks and achieves impressive results, either matching or exceeding state-of-the-art results on 21 out of 22 NLI and RTE datasets, and achieving new records on 11 and 12 NLP tasks and achieving significant advancements in generalization and performance in NLP.

A primary challenge in analyzing the atmospheres of exoplanets at a detailed level is distinguishing the effects of stellar activity from the desired signals at low resolution. To better understand this problem, a statistical study was conducted using Earth-like planets in the habitable zones of 80 stars in the vicinity of our Sun, focusing on transit depth fluctuations in specific atmospheric absorption bands. By examining the planets' signals in the presence of active regions, our research demonstrates that stellar activity can significantly obscure these signals. A key factor influencing these fluctuations is the area of active regions relative to the star, rather than their precise location. Moreover, our work reveals that cooler planets tend to be more susceptible to stellar activity than hotter planets. To counteract these effects, we developed a straightforward, observation-based method for filtering out atmospheric absorption lines originating from the planets' atmospheres by utilizing simultaneous high-resolution spectroscopy observations. Our research demonstrates that this technique can significantly minimize transit spectroscopy stellar activity effects, potentially allowing for the detection of subtle atmospheric variations related to planetary seasons.

Building on the theory of hyperbolic metrics with conical singularities, as introduced by Einstein and Karcher, we develop uniform curvature metrics on Riemann surfaces with various types of singularities, including both discrete and continuous conical singularities of different indices. The main innovation involves adapting the fixed point theorem for noncompact spaces to spaces with isometric conical singularities, enabling us to overcome the lack of continuity in the conical setting. The constructed metrics are shown to be quasi-isometric and to have singularities matching the specified indices, with an additional application involving the construction of quasi-isometric surfaces with prescribed singularities, having isometric cones.

Centipedes have an ancient lineage, dating back to the Devonian period, and their current aquatic ancestors lived around 370 million years ago. However, their terrestrial ancestors unexpectedly led their aquatic predecessors into extinction. To understand how certain smaller centipedes survive and move on the surface of water, our research focuses on these creatures' unique locomotion capabilities. By analyzing swimming mechanics and estimating the energy costs, we discovered that these small centipedes use capillary forces and gravity to remain above water, and their movement is primarily driven by the centrifugal force. As a result, these small centipedes consume less energy when moving slowly compared to faster movements, which is contrary to what is typically expected.

A high-performance computing system in the US is used to model tsunami waves created by an extraterrestrial impact, employing high-resolution simulations to study the event's spread in a complex coastal area with varying tides. To efficiently use the UTAC supercomputer, the project divides the ocean into smaller regions with varying levels of detail, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of both large-scale and region-specific tsunami behavior. A more sophisticated model is employed in areas of interest, including detailed representations of water levels and coastal area movements, while a coarser grid is used elsewhere to capture broader tsunami effects. A strategy is developed to dynamically adjust the grid size, refining it where necessary and adjusting for tidal changes, thus enabling more accurate tsunami simulations. A test case is conducted to verify this approach and assess its performance in predicting tsunami spread.

A set of 11 galaxies, detected only in the JWST's near-infrared band, with the most distant ones exceeding redshift 3, was identified. These galaxies, in the process of rapid expansion, were observed at a time when the universe was also expanding rapidly, providing a unique glimpse into early cosmic evolution. A thorough analysis of the galaxies' star-formation rates, dust content, and other properties revealed significant findings. Notably, the galaxies' masses were calculated to be in the range of 10^8-10^9 solar masses, with significant amounts of dust. A comparison of the galaxies' properties with those of local galaxies and high-redshift samples revealed that the galaxies' dust content is relatively low, suggesting that they are evolving into large, dust-filled galaxies. A series of follow-up observations of the galaxies' properties, including their star-formation rates, dust content, and masses, was conducted, with the results indicating that the galaxies' evolution is similar to that of other early cosmic galaxies.

We propose a novel four-dimensional spacetime geometry based framework for 7-dimensional gravity, similar to its 4-dimensional counterpart. This new model, similar to 4D gravity with a geometrical term, incorporates a specific 7-dimensional space geometry constructed by utilizing a novel framework involving principles of higher-dimensional topology. Through a comprehensive analysis of the resulting field equations, we find that they are inherently nonlinear and complex. Consequently, we focus on a specific class of static and spherically symmetric solutions and derive two new models of 7-dimensional space-time. Interestingly, our results show that when reducing 7-dimensional gravity with a geometrical term to 4-dimensional space-time, the resulting equations match those of 4-dimensional gravity with a cosmological term, rather than a geometrical term.

The packing of circular disks into complex shapes has long been a fundamental problem in geometry with far-reaching applications in physics, chemistry, and engineering. Research on simpler forms, specifically rectangular areas and circular blocks, has been conducted for a long time, and significant progress has been made in understanding their packings. A particularly interesting case involves the 1D packing of circular objects that can be reduced to arranging a series of circular blocks within a narrow channel. A crucial question in this area revolves around understanding the maximum number of disk arrangements that can be made when dealing with disks of two sizes and weights. In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in identifying the maximum number of such arrangements by demonstrating the feasibility of reducing any packing of two-sized disks to a limited number of arrangements for each size. Building on previous research, we further advance this area by proving that the maximum number of such arrangements can be reduced to two for each size, and more specifically, we show that the maximum number of such arrangements can be reduced to two for each size when dealing with certain types of disk weights. Our findings have significant implications for the broader field of geometry, and they open up new avenues for research on the 1D packing of circular objects.

To better understand and forecast extreme precipitation events, researchers investigated the distinct effects of different flavors of El Nino events on global precipitation patterns. Flavor events are classified by their geographical location, with onshore events characterized by widespread rainfall in the tropics and offshore events marked by a lack of rainfall in those regions. Analyzing 47 years of reanalysis data, scientists found that onshore events significantly impact precipitation more than offshore events do, with a notable difference in the intensity of rainfall during off-season periods. Specifically, they discovered a 10% increase in the area experiencing high rainfall intensity during onshore events, a difference that is most pronounced in on-season periods. Notably, these effects are most evident in on-season periods and are most pronounced in regions like the Amazon, Central Africa, and Southeast Asia. These findings will contribute to a more accurate understanding of on a regional scale, and improve precipitation forecasts.

The optical properties of solid materials, such as how they interact with light, are heavily influenced by their microscopic structure. Research has shown that materials deforming plastically, like those undergoing plastic deformation, exhibit distinct characteristics in terms of their microscopic structure compared to their elastic counterparts. The term "non-affine growth" has been used to describe a particular type of deformation found in nanomaterials, where new layers of a material grow at a different rate than the rest of the material due to the presence of an interface. In this study, researchers used computational simulations and mathematical models to predict how light scatters in systems undergoing non-affine growth, and their predictions were compared with experimental data obtained from molecular beam epitaxy grown silicon-germanium superlattices.

This research focuses on developing a population model that accounts for demographic density-dependent migration. By examining a single species with particular emphasis on the effects of aging and environmental pollution on population dynamics, we aim to establish the model's key properties, including the existence, positivity, and stability of its solutions. Through a local-Global-Stable approach, we investigate the long-term behavior of the population, including its persistence and stability, as well as the existence and stability of its interior periodic solutions under certain conditions. Furthermore, we apply bifurcation theory, including the saddle-node, Hopf, and Allee phenomena to understand the system's dynamic behavior, including the coexistence of multiple stable states, and leverage numerical simulations to validate our theoretical findings.

The concept of hypersequents, originally proposed by Negri and Timmermeyer, offers a logical framework that encompasses various features, such as weakening and contraction. To address the complexity of the hypersequent calculus, researchers have established upper and lower complexity bounds for its cut decidability, specifically 4n+1 and 4n+2, respectively. To further explore this topic, the current study expands on hypersequents by introducing a new class of calculi, known as iterated hypersequents, which allows for the inclusion of any number of weakenings and contractions. By doing so, the decision-making process regarding the number of weakenings and contractions required for cut decidability becomes evident, thereby upper bounding the complexity of the cut decision by 2n+1. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, the theory is applied to a range of specific cases, including full and contraction logics, as well as the logic of relevant logic. Moreover, this study proves the lower complexity bounds for cut decidability by examining the relevant cases, which results in 2n+1 being a precise upper bound for cut decidability across the discussed cases.

Taxonomy expansion is a widely researched natural language processing task, however, current approaches have serious shortcomings. The first issue is that many existing methods rely on knowledge bases learned in Euclidean space, which does not capture the hierarchical nature of knowledge effectively, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we propose HyperExpan, a novel method that employs knowledge bases represented in hyperbolic space to more accurately capture the geometric characteristics of taxonomy. By leveraging hyperbolic space, our approach can identify geometrically nearby knowledge items and leverage their co-occurrence relationships in text, enabling effective taxonomy expansion. The proposed method was evaluated on three publicly available datasets, and experimental results demonstrate that HyperExpan outperforms baseline methods by significant margins.

This research examines the impact of a uniform electric field on various molecular interactions, including hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, and dipole interactions. We employ computational methods to accurately model the effects of electric fields on structure and energy. Our findings reveal that electric fields can significantly influence energy and the stability of molecular complexes, particularly when two strong electric field sources are present. We discover that electric fields can notably alter the energy landscape of these interactions, leading to new local minima in energy and shifting existing minima. These results have important implications for our understanding of force fields, protein folding, and the accurate prediction of molecular behavior under external influences. Our research highlights the need for further development and optimization of force fields to capture the effects of electric fields on a wide range of molecular interactions.

The fourth revolution in industry greatly enhances production systems flexibility and variability. By leveraging data-driven technologies, companies can now integrate real-time data into decision-making processes, yielding highly dynamic and optimized scheduling systems. However, the rapid growth of data-driven scheduling systems in manufacturing raises two major challenges: real-time data's reliability and accuracy. While real-time data is becoming increasingly accessible, its reliability and accuracy are uncertain, posing significant hurdles to decision-making processes. To address this issue, we developed a novel Bayesian K-nearest neighbor (KBN-KNN) algorithm that leverages real-time data's temporal patterns to identify and address data quality issues. This algorithm's effectiveness was demonstrated through numerical examples and a real-world case study on a simulated production line.

In this research, we establish a framework for measuring the robustness of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) using the STL framework, with a focus on systems susceptible to malicious cyber interference. We represent potential attacks as a stochastic process influencing CPS behavior, with the robustness criterion evaluating an STL formula and multiple possible outcomes resulting from the probabilistic process. A new concept, Stochastic Sign Robustness, is introduced, where we evaluate the reliability of an STL formula's logical structure, considering the probabilities of its components at each time point. We demonstrate how to calculate the robustness criterion of an STL formula and introduce the attack influence matrix, which quantifies the impact of attacks on CPS state transitions, with a demonstration in a robotic CPS example.

A new search strategy for detecting dark matter is proposed by analyzing fluctuations in the motion of ground-based transport networks equipped with accelerometers. Focusing on large-scale networks consisting of buses and trains, this approach targets specific predictions made within certain hidden sector models featuring a light fermion and a pseudoscalar mediator. Acceleration data collected during ground transport can be transformed into vertical acceleration records, comparable to those obtained from stationary networks, such as those on ships or parked vehicles. However, ground transportation networks have distinct advantages in detecting fermion-pair production through couplings to nucleons, particularly in urban environments with high construction activity resulting from tunnel excavations and subway expansions. A preliminary feasibility assessment suggests that a year's worth of data from city centers could confirm or refute predicted hidden sector models with fermion masses up to a certain limit and coupling strengths within a specific range.

A nonlinear diffusion equation is analyzed on complete geodesic manifolds with gradients. An established heat equation based method was previously proposed by Zhang and their colleagues. This study further develops and generalizes that work by introducing a novel gradient approximation and proving its convergence for weak solutions. Furthermore, the article addresses the existence of gradients by verifying specific weak solution assumptions and employs an additional gradient approximation to demonstrate the existence of gradients on manifolds with geodesic properties.

The origins and nature of faint radio sources in the cosmos are still not fully understood.  By utilizing a novel method called stacking, researchers can gain insights into the average physical characteristics of these distant sources, which in turn can inform models of their underlying physical source types.  By focusing on a specific range of angular dimensions, from a few to hundreds of kiloparsecs, a study has found that radio sources with higher angular dimensions have higher average redshifts, higher average luminosity, and higher average radio power.  Moreover, it was discovered that radio sources with higher angular dimensions have higher average core-to-lobe flux ratios, which suggests that larger sources are more likely to be FR-II in shape.  Furthermore, it was found that radio sources with higher angular dimensions have lower average Emission Measure (EM) values, which suggests a scenario where radio sources with higher Luminosity and higher Jet Power are more likely to have fringed spectra with higher core-to-lobe flux ratios.  These findings are consistent with a scenario in which larger sources have higher luminosity and higher luminosity-dependent redshift trends.  Moreover, it was discovered that radio sources with higher angular dimensions have higher luminosity-dependent redshift trends.  These findings are consistent with a scenario in which larger sources have higher luminosity-dependent redshift trends.
