Currently, German speech data is largely utilized by several companies, limiting access for researchers. To address this, we developed and released a new German语 automated speech recognition system based on the Open-Source Kaldi framework. This model achieves word error rates of 6.2% and 7.5% on two testing datasets, demonstrating comparable performance to proprietary models, while significantly reducing resource consumption by Kaldi.

The 30 Doradus nebula, located within the Large Magellanic Cloud, is home to a striking collection of star clusters. This paper examines the Be-type stars, fast-rotating B stars with distinctive gaseous equatorial discs, by analyzing data from the 30 Doradus region. An investigation of spectral lines reveals that these Be-stars exhibit broad H$\beta$ absorption features, while emission lines are narrower. This study categorizes Be-stars into single stars, binary systems, and potential multiple systems. It also analyzes the relationship between rotational velocity and mass for these stars. A comparison of temperature, luminosity, and mass to theoretical models reveals that these Be-stars are over-rotating. This paper's findings are comparable to those of similar studies on Be-stars in other 30 Doradus star clusters.

To improve the performance of data-driven Inverse Text Normalization (ITN), we investigate data augmentation techniques, focusing on two key aspects: creating diverse training data and increasing its volume. Various methods are applied to improve full ITN models by preserving readability and variety in generated numbers. The effectiveness of these techniques is evaluated on the Wikipedia dataset and ADS-17k. The results indicate that ensemble learning can effectively leverage augmented data to boost model performance.

This paper explores the Faber-Krahn inequality for the eigenvalues of the Hermite operator, subject to specific boundary constraints. By applying a symmetrization technique to an original result, we demonstrate that among all domains within R^n, the ball yields the smallest eigenvalues for this Hermite-modified problem, aligning with a known result from Bandle and Zou in the case of unconstrained boundary conditions.

The success of neural tangent kernels (NTKs) in understanding overparameterized neural networks lies in their ability to linearize these networks around a solution found at training time. This study introduces the neural tangent kernel's limitations in capturing class exchangeability, and proposes a Korkinikhadzhiev kernel as a better replacement to depict the joint behavior of a single class more accurately. This improved kernel can accelerate the training of neural networks by focusing the gradient direction on a specific class and can serve as a better classifier by dividing a trained kernel into separate components that represent different classes. Numerical results validate the effectiveness of introducing this new kernel.

The abundance of topological research in condensed matter physics is largely due to the emergence of robust topological phases and their accompanying phase transitions, where protecting symmetries play a vital role in ensuring their stability. In particular, research on non-Hermitian systems has gained significant attention, particularly in exploring the unique characteristics of non-Hermitian topological phases. Our research examines the topological structure of a one-dimensional non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where we initially identified a unique phase characterized by the presence of an exceptional ring and complete band inversion, along with a topology-based edge mode under open boundary conditions. Interestingly, we discovered that when considering the non-Hermitian case with open boundaries, conventional topological theories break down. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a unique phase transition occurs when considering the effect of non-Hermiticity correlations in the one-dimensional Hermitian system, ultimately leading to the elimination of complete band inversion and topological edge modes under open boundary conditions. Our findings emphasize the crucial role of non-Hermiticity correlations in determining the stability of non-Hermitian topological phases and suggest that these correlations are a fundamental aspect of these unique phases.

To incorporate distinctive speaker characteristics into synthetic speech, a
deep learning model is utilized, demonstrating its application with a focus on
a child's voice. The model's performance is assessed through a listener test,
revealing its capacity to generate characteristics that go beyond mere speaker
identification. The analysis also examines how well the models preserve key
acoustic traits when creating new voices and how their output compares to
actual child speech patterns.

We've developed a unique Dark Matter model, incorporating $A_4$ symmetry and a global $211$ fermion parity, in conjunction with the minimal $B-L$ extension of the Standard Model. Our model features modular $A_4$ symmetry, where key parameters, such as neutrino mass differences and mixing angles, are linked to the modular lambda function. This model also predicts a $CP$ even, second-order, see-saw see-saw mechanism for neutrinos. As a result, we anticipate a correlation between the neutrino mixing angle $\theta_{13}$ and the Dark Matter relic density. Furthermore, we've discovered that the model can be tested using both direct and indirect Dark Matter detection searches as well as the LHC, particularly when the Higgs portal is suppressed by a large $A_4$ symmetry breaking parameter.

Building on the theoretical framework of Triaxial Liquid Drop Model (LLM) and incorporating Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle with a minimal length parameter, we develop a quantum model. By minimizing the free energy, we obtain self-consistent equations which we solve to determine the properties of nuclei. Our results demonstrate a direct relationship between the quantized deformation levels and a nucleus's shape. For spherical nuclei, energy levels align with established findings. However, as spherical symmetry breaks down into deformed states, we observe a correlation between minimal length and a nucleus's collective motion amplitude. This correlation reveals that the minimal length concept effectively curbs collective movement in nuclei. We found that triangular rotors possess the most restricted collective movement, whereas double rotor systems are less constrained by the minimal length concept.

Recently, Golay complementary arrays were proposed, and they possess favorable radar characteristics and versatile applications. This work proposes novel designs of Golay complementary arrays via polyphase filter methods, and it specifically presents examples of Golay complementary arrays with phase shifts of $0,\pi/4$ and those with complex coefficients, achieving a high phase efficiency. The proposed designs are systematic and can be used to generate Golay complementary arrays of various sizes.

Incorporating deep learning into change detection methods in image analysis has gained significant attention due to its ability to efficiently process and interpret complex images. Despite this, designing deep neural networks specifically for change detection remains a challenge, particularly when dealing with detailed spectral information found in hyperspectral images. This work introduces a novel method using unsupervised change detection through deep neural networks, specifically tailored for hyperspectral images. By leveraging a deep feature fusion deep convolutional neural network, this approach captures the rich spectral information present in these images, which single-band analysis methods cannot adequately address. Additionally, the development of a novel neuromodulation mechanism, the Feature Fusion Deep Convolutional Neuromodulators (FFDCN), enables the network to be trained without labeled data. When applied to hyperspectral images, our proposed method yields superior results compared to other leading change detection techniques.

A comprehensive theoretical framework for molecular fluids has been developed, 
revealing a correlation between the configuration integral and viscosity via a configuration viscosity coefficient. This has been successfully tested for various ensemble types, including NVT, NVE, NPT, and the microcanonical ensemble. To validate the model's applicability, we analyzed a diverse range of molecular fluids, encompassing both real substances and theoretical models. Notably, we found that the configuration viscosity coefficient serves as a reliable predictor of the fluid's viscosity at high pressures, especially for the kinetic theory for linear and spherical fluids. Furthermore, we discovered a significant link between the residual entropy and viscosity in weakly anisotropic molecular fluids, a phenomenon that we demonstrated through a comparison with experimental data and simulation results for molecular fluids, as well as an analysis of the implications for the choice of potential models.

The standard $\Lambda CDM$ model of cosmology is expanded into a cyclical model featuring repeated periods of expansion, contraction, and bounce-back cycles.  A comparative analysis of the oscillating cosmology within the context of observationally constrained parameters has been conducted, with the resulting cyclical model predictions for the cosmic microwave background presented.  This analysis includes an examination of type Ia supernovae data, with the findings suggesting that the current cyclical model is consistent with data for up to ten oscillations, a scenario which is not in conflict with the current data.  Furthermore, the study highlights potential distinctions between the cyclical and standard models, with the latter exhibiting different behavior in the expansion of type Ia supernovae and distinct differences in cosmic microwave background power spectra, particularly in the oscillation patterns and damping tail.

A hidden-variable version of the Invariant-set theory is analyzed, which asserts that preexisting hidden variables have no influence on the experimental outcome. By examining this version's properties, we find that the statistical equality condition that underpins it is superdeterministic in nature. To avoid introducing circular reasoning, we propose necessary conditions for non-superdeterminism and show that the statistical equality condition fails to meet these criteria. The model's internal consistency is then tested through the Bell scenario and the QBism framework. The examination of these two scenarios yields different results: the derivation of a contradiction in the former and validation of the former in the latter.

Keyphrase spotting refers to the process of generating a concise description consisting of several words that accurately captures the essence of an input. In the context of IoT devices, where computational resources are often limited, there is a need for lightweight keyphrase spotting models. In this paper, we introduce a novel neural network architecture, which is specifically designed for providing fast and accurate inference on small IoT devices. The proposed model, which is built upon the BERT architecture, has been shown to outperform a baseline model in terms of both computational efficiency and term preservation, as evidenced by experiments conducted on three publicly available datasets. The accompanying code and model weights can be accessed at https://github.com/alexandrejean/kps-ipv

This report outlines the foundational steps for a potential application of holomorphic and anti-holomorphic dimer models to the simulation of fermions influenced by background gauge fields on two-dimensional square lattices. Potential connections to the description of topological insulators and superconductors are explored as a bonus perspective.

Working with categorical data in high-dimensional data sets is often complicated because there are a limited number of distinct data points for each variable, data sets tend to have many parameters, and standard models are not easily interpretable. To address this issue, we've developed enhanced versions of Group Lasso and Group Adaboost, incorporating the benefits of these well-known methods, including the ability to handle high-dimensional data, automatic feature selection, and clear interpretations. These improved models outperform their original counterparts as well as the best existing cluster-based multiclass classification methods on many high-dimensional categorical data sets, based on experiments conducted on both synthetic data and datasets sourced from a variety of real-world sources.

We present T-Visor, a virtualization manager specifically designed for embedded real-time systems, incorporating hardware virtualization capabilities. T-visor addresses the limitations of existing virtualization managers by optimizing resource allocation and ensuring the timeliness of virtualized system operations. We demonstrate the suitability of T-visor for a wide range of scenarios, including systems running multiple hypervisors, and provide the necessary tools for accurately measuring the resource overhead introduced by virtualized scheduling. Furthermore, we utilize T-visor to create a dual-hypervisor system, integrating it with Xen, and develop a comprehensive framework for ensuring real-time performance, along with extensive validation through empirical analysis.

A primary issue in digital image processing is joining panoramic images to create detailed multi-view 3D representations. Multi-view 3D reconstruction, however, poses several challenges, including excessive memory usage and excessive computation time due to the large number of images involved. Excessive parameters also lead to overfitting and difficulty in generalizing across different subjects. 

To address these issues, we propose a novel gravity-based approach to panoramic image joining. By limiting image joining options to a minimal global subset, our method significantly reduces its memory and computational requirements. This allows it to process large image collections from multiple views on a single GPU efficiently. Furthermore, our method optimizes performance by selectively joining panoramic images only when needed.

Evaluating our approach on the Linemod dataset demonstrates that it achieves a minimal global panorama with a high mean IoU score of 0.73, outperforming a panoramic image joining method that considers all options. This impressive performance is achieved even with drastic reductions in memory and computational requirements.

Chimeric states state-wide state synchronization within groups of independently oscillating units, where inter-group connections are insufficient to achieve uniform oscillation. This phenomenon occurs with units exhibiting random or uniform random parameters that influence their oscillation frequency. Using analytical techniques including analytical population eigenfunctions and a stochastic approach, we have identified stable chimeria conditions for two large populations coupled at their peaks. This includes identification of parameter ranges supporting chimeric existence and exploration of potential transitions out of these states. Notably, leaving chimera states can result in either complete oscillation desynchronization or near-uniformity, offering insight into oscillation patterns transition mechanisms.

We examine the issue of developing a controller for an uncertain dynamic system, even when the uncertainty is dynamically influenced by the controller, based on a probabilistic model of the system. To address this challenge, we propose a new method that iteratively refines a controller for the probabilistic model, ensuring robustness against uncertainty in the true dynamic system, by balancing model accuracy and robustness. This approach is evaluated through numerical simulations, including scenarios with non-linear dynamic uncertainty.

A new category called the multi-layer diagram category is defined. Diagrams within this category can be linked to higher algebraic structures operating on multi-layer diagrams, which comprise elements of different group elements arranged in sequence. For any positive integer n greater than or equal to 2, the resulting category is finite, semi-simple, and weakly symmetric, possessing a higher Frobenius algebra property that is symmetric and special. Additionally, a condition is established, under which the category is rigid.

A newly established concept of mutual information "reflected entropy" is explored for arbitrary random tensor networks with multiple tensored gauge theory groups. Analytical calculations of reflected entropy reveal that the information flow is closely linked to the longest paths within the dual network's structure, particularly in tensor networks composed of multiple groups, and also to the spectral properties of a dual lattice as seen in planar network models. These findings are confirmed by direct numerical verification.

Systems that transmit genetic information are fundamental to diverse natural and artificial processes, driving their evolution and development. In an effort to understand how this transmission occurs, we've shifted the focus from pre-existing structures to those that emerge through stochastic interactions between a system and its environment. However, these spontaneously formed patterns often disappear due to random fluctuations and environmental interference. To address this issue, we're exploring self-organizing patterns that can resist noise and persist across generations, enabling information to be passed down from one generation to the next.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of the three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non system, particularly when $\alpha$ is set to 0.15, by producing and analyzing the bifurcation diagrams and attractors of this system. Our study reveals that the system exhibits various forms of chaotic behavior and we visualize these dynamics using the band and in-lieft projection algorithms. As a result, we can depict the attractors of this system in three-dimensional space and observe that they share similarities with those of the classic H\'{e}non system.

Researchers are still working to uncover the quantum structure of gravity and their current theories have their roots in the gravity's geometric properties, specifically the Poincaré group's holonomy. Gravitational gravity theory proposes that gravity can be represented through a spin connection, whose properties on a closed manifold uniquely identify the gravitational holonomy. This concept has significant implications for spin foams and other models of quantum gravity. This research paper proves that a closed manifold's gravitational holonomy uniquely corresponds with an equivalence class of spin connections, effectively categorizing states in the Poincaré gauge theory based on their topological properties.

We analyze the statistical behavior of 2- and 3-hook length distributions in ordinary partitions, specifically focusing on the behavior as the number of parts in each goes to infinity with a consistent relationship between the number of parts and the size of the partition.

Researchers have successfully created a spin-electron quantum tunneling system using a single atom of $^{133}\textrm{Cs}$ and implemented the Larmor clock to measure tunneling time. By examining the spin tunneling duration as a function of the Cs electron's polarization state, we developed a quantum theoretical model to explain the underlying spin fluctuations that influence tunneling time. Our experiment yielded a constant tunneling time of approximately 1.5 ns, regardless of the Cs electron's polarization state. Furthermore, the experimental results matched the predicted outcomes from our theoretical model.

We have developed a straightforward approach for deriving the leading twist light cone distribution functions of nonrelativistic mesons, which were previously uncertain about their existence. Our analysis includes both the distribution of leading twist wave functions and the parton distribution and fragmentation functions at the leading twist. Furthermore, we have derived key scaling relations for these distribution functions and computed the evolution of wave functions using the DGLAP equation, showing that they reach a stable asymptotic state.

The study of quantum operators linked to differential equations of Operators' Method is a significant area of research for solving nonlinear quantum equations, particularly for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation governing Bose-Einstein condensates. Research on the GP equation began in the 1980s to investigate the phenomenon of Bose condensation in low-dimensional systems, with the discovery of self-trapping. The GP equation has been shown to be associated with a family of nonlinear operators, including those related to Hermite polynomials. By exploring newGP(s) operators and their properties, new sets of orthogonal functions and differential equations are being explored to better understand the behavior of Bose-Einstein condensates. The study of wave functions and probability density of a BEC requires novel approaches, such as the newGP(s) operator, to better model low-dimensional systems.
We provide a basic overview of the BMS geometry and double soft gravitational theorem.

Learning from a series of unrelated tasks without knowing when one task ends and the next begins, is known as Continual Learning. Current methods, however, struggle with this challenge and tend to experience "catastrophic forgetting," where the model loses previously learned information. To overcome this issue, we propose NEO, an Online Ensemble method that leverages neural networks, allowing it to adapt to new tasks without needing task boundaries and without storing past experience. NEO's architecture, inspired by distillation, enables efficient learning even with limited data, and can handle large-scale tasks like ImageNet-level problems. Furthermore, NEO's selection mechanism helps identify the tasks at hand and utilizes a mean queue to retain older task information. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that NEO outperforms existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness in this scenario.

We introduce a novel class of geometric objects known as generalized $G$-forms with associated metrics. Our proposed definition encompasses conventional forms as well as form-dependent metrics. A specific instance of these generalized objects is the Dirac current associated with a spacetime metric. We establish relationships between generalized forms and their corresponding metrics and derive a generalized version of the Ricci flat condition. Our analysis demonstrates that both the Einstein and Ricci flat conditions can be expressed elegantly in terms of generalized objects. Additionally, we examine the distinct features of the generalized objects in dimension four and link them to the Weyl current measure, revealing novel ways to express spacetime properties such as the Kretschmann measure and Poynting vector measure exclusively through generalized objects in four dimensions.

This study examines the conditions under which certain permutation polynomials are operative in over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. By establishing novel results for permutation polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$, we derive invariance outcomes for total permutation polynomials within permutation linear sets in $\mathrm{Sp}(6, q) / 2$.

The Deep Belief System (DBS) is a form of unsupervised deep learning network, which is an extension of the belief-regression model. Our study aims to utilize DBS for automatic classification of intestinal parasites in fecal samples, after image enhancement and preprocessing. The proposed model achieves a 96.6% accuracy on publicly available data, outperforming other methods by providing a simplified graphical user interface for easier deployment.

This work introduces novel numerical techniques for resolving a category of non-zero-sum continuous-time dynamic problems, specifically investment and reinsurance control problems within a regime-switching jump-diffusion model framework, to maximize team performance. By leveraging regime-switching dynamics and utilizing the connection between performance differences and Maxwell systems, we develop a grid-based numerical approach that enables the approximation of all control functions simultaneously through grid-based control functions. We further establish the convergence of these approximations in the $L^2$-sense and provide a practical method for solving the resulting finite-dimensional problem. Our approach is validated through numerical experiments demonstrating its efficiency.

This study proposes a unique approach to controlling Underactuated Quadrotors, combining an advanced algorithm, the Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm (PiDSA), with a filtering technique, the Genetic Filter (GF), to optimize flight stability and efficiency. By integrating PiDSA with a two-loop stabilization strategy, we achieve precise and efficient control over each axis of the Quadrotor. Furthermore, we utilize the GF to accurately estimate key state variables, overcoming limitations of traditional filters in handling non-linear systems. Our proposed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional alternatives, showcasing its potential for robust and versatile underactuated systems control.

A comprehensive mathematical model has been developed to describe low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, encompassing three-meson vertices, propagators, form factors, and amplitudes. This framework enables the separation of the complex amplitude into distinct components through rigorous mathematical derivation. Three key principles underpin the model, namely unitarity, analyticity, and a specific constraint on the far-off-shell form factor. By applying these principles, the model successfully reduces the eight-component scattering amplitude to four essential variables at the physical nucleon pole, thereby providing essential information for deriving low-energy pion-nucleon observables. Moreover, the model demonstrates that low-energy pion-nucleon reactions are fundamentally governed by just three critical variables, namely three-meson form factors, propagators, and a specific constraint. Consequently, the constraint can be effectively replaced by the narrow resonance approximation. Several predictions and applications are discussed, including a new prediction regarding pion-nucleon positron annihilation at low energies.

Over the past decade, several CMS detectors underwent upgrades to enhance their capabilities before the Large Hadron Collider restarted in 2022 for the High-Luminosity era.  A crucial component in this upgrade is the upgrade of the pixel system, which currently faces challenges due to increased radiation damage and higher data rates of up to 760 Hz.  To address these issues, the CMS team developed new detection and tracking algorithms to process the data generated by the pixel system, which will be compared against the old ones during data analysis.  These new algorithms were initially tested on the CMS pilot pixel blade data, which will be processed during a simulated run that mimics the real LHC environment at a data set of 30 fb^-1.  By comparing the results from these tests, the CMS team will be able to verify the efficiency of the new algorithms and ensure their readiness for deployment in the main detector before the HL-LHC begins operations.

Active galactic nuclei in distant galaxies are believed to be regulated by complex interactions between their central black holes and surrounding starbursts, black holes, gas, and dust. By comparing observed active galactic nuclei spectra to templates representing various star formation and active galactic nuclei host galaxy templates, researchers can determine the structure of their host galaxies. However, determining whether galaxies in the redshift range 0.1-0.6 are dominated by stars, dust, or active galactic nuclei nuclei is challenging. To address this, we employed machine learning to establish boundaries separating purely stellar spectra from those containing significant active galactic nuclei and dust components, and used it to classify the host galaxy structure of 22,000 galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey. Our findings reveal that approximately 40% of galaxies at a distance of 0.1 to 0.6 are classified as having a particular structure, and our results suggest that small black holes tend to reside in galaxies with a particular structure, whereas large black holes tend to reside in galaxies with a particular structure. Furthermore, our findings suggest that galaxies with a particular structure are characterized by fewer dust components and lower dust temperatures.

Nucleons within a nucleus can engage in brief, intense interactions known as nuclear short-range correlations, resulting in distinct high-energy relationships between pairs of nucleons. These correlations can be manifested in various quantum states associated with high relative momentum among nucleons. This review examines theoretical approaches to understanding these correlations, focusing on their application within phase-space representations such as quantum phase operators' expectation values. Furthermore, it showcases findings from quantum Monte Carlo~calculations, correlating short-range correlations with the high-momentum structure factors, two-nucleon separation distributions, momentum distributions, and missing energy spectra.

Deep complex networks have been applied to resolve issues in signal processing and DSP, where input data is inherently complex-valued, and outputs must also be of a complex nature to be effective in solving these problems. However, the limitations of current complex-valued activation functions hinder the efficacy of deep complex networks in downstream tasks. The similarity of outputs from adjacent network layers, despite differing input data, can lead to information loss and signal degradation in these networks. We propose the complex rectified sine as an alternative to traditional complex activation functions such as the complex sign function, and demonstrate its effectiveness in deep complex networks, and compare it with existing alternatives such as Gabor and Relu functions.

The non-linear QCD evolution at small-$x$ beyond the saturation momentum $Q_s$ was initially studied in deep inelastic ep scattering during the 1990s due to increased sensitivity at HERA. Subsequent research revealed evidence for saturation effects at various energy levels, particularly at low $x_B$ values near $10^{-3}$, where $Q_s$ was probed by experiments at HERA. At higher $x_B$, $Q_s$ may have been inaccessible by these experiments. Conversely, heavy ion collisions at RHIC and the future FCC-hh may probe $Q_s$ more effectively. Saturation and geometric scaling have also been found to apply to hadron production, particularly to single-parton production at RHIC's energies, influenced by non-linear QCD evolution and $Q_s$. Moreover, geometric scaling has been found to apply to hadron production in proton-proton collisions. Investigation into the origin of this phenomenon across different energy regimes and processes is necessary.

The low metallicity of stars has long been associated with large amplitude variations in brightness, yet the underlying reasons for this phenomenon remain unclear. We have identified two primary factors contributing to this variation: (a) a high proportion of outer ionized calcium layers in stars containing 10-12 hydrogen-like, even-atomic-number stars, and (b) a lower overall envelope opacity resulting from reduced heavy metal abundance. These factors are particularly significant in B-type subdwarf Oe stars, which are expected to exhibit the largest amplitude variations. Notably, a lower metallicity increases amplitude in all stars, but it has the most pronounced effect on low-metallicity stars with a helium core and a hydrogen-rich envelope. This study provides the first detailed explanation of why low metallicity results in increased pulsation amplitudes.

Machine learning models are widely used in education, finance, and marketing, but their effectiveness depends on varying contextual factors and operational settings. Current research has mainly focused on improving machine learning models' predictive capabilities, but their sensitivity to changes is often overlooked. This study introduces a novel methodology and accompanying tools to systematically evaluate machine learning models' responsiveness to variations in context and operational parameters. Leveraging a widely accepted machine learning library, we examine the importance of features within models, revealing that models can have distinct sensitivities to different inputs and input ranges. Utilizing an educational dataset sourced from nearly 2000 individuals' responses to a financial literacy survey, we analyze the impact of key characteristics on model sensitivity. Our research highlights the necessity of incorporating the sensitivity of machine learning models in education, finance, and marketing decision-making processes.

This research introduces a groundbreaking approach to accelerate Machine Intelligence with Quantum Annealing, specifically using the QA-SQUID model. By applying the principles of quantum mechanics, this model achieves accelerated learning compared to traditional Machine Learning models. In the first stage of development, the SQUID-based energy function is incorporated into the MAQP model, allowing binary neurons to learn continuously rather than discretely. This leads to significant advancements in learning speed and accuracy compared to binary neural networks. Furthermore, this model's adaptability allows it to be utilized in various applications, such as brain-inspired computing and simulated annealing. Notably, quantum annealing's connection to continuous training techniques enables the formulation of an iterative process that approximates the quantum Hamiltonian's ground state, facilitating the transition from quantum to continuous machines.

This research paper focuses on almost contact manifolds and examines points where a submanifold has specific geometric properties, called pointwise semi-inclined angles with its tangent planes relative to those of a wider manifold it's a part of. We derive expressions for when a submanifold can be considered part of a particular type of multi-layered structure and find that this can only happen when the submanifold has a certain inherent symmetry, known as being a pointwise semi-sphere.

A critical challenge in low energy nuclear recoil detection, particularly for low-energy nuclear recoil (LRN) detection, lies in the identification of recombination processes that occur at very low energies. The research we conducted recently focused on developing an innovative method utilizing the photoluminescence properties of color centers embedded in nanodiamonds to detect and identify low-energy nuclear recoils caused by ionizing radiation. Our experiments were performed using a neutron beam, and we demonstrated the direct observation of low-energy recoils affecting 14C isotopes. The resulting data showed a well-defined double Gaussian distribution centered around 15-25 photons, and our research also demonstrated the distinction between nuclear and electronic recoils through an optimized detection system employing single photon counting. The PALEOCCENE collaboration has been established to explore the potential of this technology for the detection of dark matter and other advanced nuclear physics research applications, with a focus on pushing the sensitivity limits of passive low energy recoil detection, ultimately contributing to the broader search for hidden cosmic phenomena.

We conduct simulated experiments on a type of effective particle called colloidal molecules, made up of smaller particles influenced by thermal and external activity-based forces. Our study reveals that these force-driven particles exhibit peculiar behaviors, such as crossing regions unfavorable to them, to achieve an equilibrium state where they concentrate in areas of higher activity. Moreover, when these particle groups, or superaggregates, form, they exhibit similar behaviors, resulting in the emergence of a macro-advective phenomenon that can be used to build active machines.

Our research on experimentally observed magnetorotons in fractional quantum Hall films reveals a surprising connection between their numbers and a fundamental property of their fractional quantum hall states, specifically the denominator of their least simplified fraction. This discovery led us to explore the energy structure of magnetorotons in more complex systems with multiple levels of complexity, and we found a remarkable set of patterns that apply to these systems, encompassing various types of Hall states and higher-order rotations. These patterns, which have been mathematically proven, provide new insights into the behaviors of these systems, such as how they interact and change under external influences, and how their components combine and separate in specific ways, all of which have significant implications for our understanding of these unique quantum hall states.

Identifying and analyzing outbreaks on networks within epidemiology is a crucial task, with well-established methods primarily focusing on creating spatial outbreak clusters. This study develops a novel, non-spatial approach to partitioning networks based on outbreak data, using novel spatial pattern detection methods that are either adapted for network use or specifically designed for this purpose. Two data sets are analyzed to illustrate the effectiveness of this method, showing that it performs competitively in terms of identifying spatial patterns while outperforming other approaches in predicting outbreak spread and clustering validation metrics. The proposed method's implementation is available through the R package, networkclustminer.

Developing efficient algorithms for source detection and light curves is crucial for future CMB experiments like CMB-SID and SPT-3G. We present a straightforward yet powerful method to eliminate non-Gaussian anomalies in full sky maps, which is based on a modified likelihood analysis. This method is applied in a simulated analysis using data from the SPT-3G camera, which observed the CMB near the Cygnus star complex. We found that our approach is effective in a wide range of signal strengths and accurately recovers CMB values, which is further supported by a specific example from the Cygnus region data where it successfully removes an anomaly linked to a dust plume, resulting in a notable decrease in map variance. This method can be applied to future data and will help ensure unbiased results in likelihood analyses of CMB maps.

Current goal-conditioned reinforcement learning techniques struggle with specific language inputs due to the ambiguity of word meanings and environmental references. Overcoming this challenge is vital for developing AI that interacts naturally with humans. This study introduces an approach to resolve ambiguity by integrating knowledge from diverse vocabulary sources. Specifically, we (1) employ transfer learning for general environmental concepts using models trained on diverse datasets, and (2) utilize multi-task learning within goal-conditioned reinforcement learning for environment-specific attributes. The proposed method is demonstrated through complex goal-setting tasks in simulated robot navigation environments, yielding substantial performance enhancements.

Quantum information processing relies on channels, which are described by quantum operations. Direct evidence for quantum tunneling has been gathered by using a "quantum camera" based on interference patterns. Similarly, we propose a method called quantum shadow procedure (SP) tomography to analyze quantum channels. In this approach, we use probes that interact with the channel in an idealized way to create distinguishable interference patterns, which reveal the channel's properties. By applying NP tomography to these probes, we can reconstruct their images and directly obtain information about quantum states and operators. An experiment demonstrating this concept was performed using superconducting qubits, which showed that our method accurately distinguishes between different types of quantum channels and recovers their properties from interference patterns. By using machine learning, we found that NP tomography of probes is essential to reduce errors in channel measurements and achieve accurate results that outperform traditional measurement techniques. By using machine learning, we found that our method outperforms traditional channel discrimination methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

For the Euclidean ball of a specified radius, a lower bound has been exactly determined, below which the Cheeger constant of all spatial domains must fall. In contrast, it was previously demonstrated that a certain upper bound exists, characterized by a specific diameter-related value multiplied by a constant, divided by the area of the domain's cross-section, with a positive, fixed constant, and radius, divided by the domain's radius, to a specific power. In our study, this upper bound was improved, resulting in a more accurate estimate.

This study explores the optimal flight path design for applications constrained by time, with a particular focus on the agent-scouting scenario. In this context, an unmanned aerial vehicle with limited battery life must visit various agents spread across a confined area before they expire. By modeling this problem as a Markov Decision Process, we aim to maximize the number of agents successfully visited. Given the computational complexity of finding exact solutions, we develop two heuristic approaches to generate near-optimal policies. To our knowledge, this is the first application of Markov Decision Processes to agent-scouting problems. Two extensive simulations were conducted to evaluate the performance of these proposed methods.

A novel renormalization group method is developed to study the low-energy properties of bilayer graphite with long-range Coulomb interactions at zero temperature. By transforming the model into an effective single-layer graphite model in the infrared limit, we establish that the bilayer splitting significantly influences the low-energy behavior. Specifically, enhanced bilayer splitting results in increased metallic character within the energy range near the Fermi level. In contrast, a reduced bilayer splitting leads to low-energy electron-electron correlations that promote semimetallic characteristics. Moreover, in the absence of bilayer splitting, the system undergoes a phase transition from a semimetal to a semiconducting state at low energies due to correlation effects. Additionally, our findings suggest that in the energy range near the Fermi level, many-body effects enhance the bilayer splitting when it's initially present.

This study investigates the impact of temperature on the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 endohedral fullerenes, which were exohedrally functionalized with hydrogen, fluorine, and chlorine atoms and then adsorbed onto h-BN/Ni(111) surfaces. By using scanning tunneling microscopy, researchers observed that at 77 K, both axial and equatorial conformers of Sc2TbN@C80 were co-existed on the surface. However, as the temperature increased to 300 K, only the equatorial conformer remained. Furthermore, it was discovered that the hydrogen, fluorine, and chlorine functional groups facilitated the conversion from the axial conformer to the equatorial conformer through a surface-parallel rotation mechanism.

This study introduces a novel compact encryption algorithm that leverages
hardware acceleration to enhance security for IoT devices while minimizing
power consumption. Utilizing the STM32Cube.AI toolchain, the algorithm is
implemented on an ARM Cortex-M4 processor, where a key aspect involves replacing
AES instructions with lightweight cryptographic modules to facilitate dynamic key
change capabilities not supported by hardware acceleration. This research evaluates
the performance of the algorithm compared to existing STM32Cube.AI configurations,
resulting in a 50% reduction in power consumption.

The Ramsey sequence measurement technique is a widely used precision method in modern quantum metrology, but its usual fixed-length approach doesn't optimize results efficiently. A new method called sequential Bayesian experiment arrangement can be employed to dynamically adjust the number of Ramsey measurements in real-time, allowing for more efficient and adaptive experiments. This method's properties, including its non-invasive nature and symmetry, are explored in detail and compared with other strategies like adaptive phase arrangements. Numerical simulations demonstrate that these adjusted phase arrangements outperform traditional methods, particularly when measuring small signals with high noise levels.

Network centrality metrics assess node importance by analyzing relationships between connected and non-connected nodes. A new multi-scale metric for network centrality has been developed based on multi-scale geometric properties. The matrix Gromov centrality measures central information flow between a node and others through a Gaussian-weighted matrix, where a key value, Gromov centrality, quantifies central nodes by their tendency towards shorter geometric paths. The proposed metric is versatile as it can be applied to both weighted and unweighted networks at various geodesic distances, providing insights into central nodes' influence and connections.

A new gravitation model based on a static, axisymmetric metric is proposed, where the line element is defined as $ds^2 = A(r,z) c^2 dt^2 - B(r,z) [d r^2 + r^2 d \phi^2] - z^2 dt^2$.  The functions $A(r,z)$ and $B(r,z)$ are determined by solving the Einstein field equations for the given metric.  The model is shown to be consistent with existing observations, and the Einstein field equations are solved for the given metric.  The resulting solutions are shown to reduce to the Schwarzschild solution for the given metric.  The model is shown to be consistent with existing observations, and the Einstein field equations are solved for the given metric.  The resulting solutions are shown to reduce to the Schwarzschild solution for the given metric.

Given matrix operators $A$ and $B$ strictly equivalent, an associated relation $\mathcal{R}$ exists such that for any matrix coefficient $C$ of $A$, there is a corresponding matrix coefficient $D$ of $B$, with strict equivalence, and these new findings explore the properties of such bundles in more detail.
The K-theory cohomology of the twisted cylinder exhibits a K-theory-T-Duality.

We develop an efficient algorithm to represent any d-dimensional metric space over at most 2^(O(d^2) log^2(d)) elements with minimal loss in distances. This representation, which approximates every distance within a factor of O(d), enables the creation of metric graphs with low treewidth and minor-width in logarithmic factors of graph parameters. This outcome also leads to a breakthrough in creating treewidth representations of planar graphs graphs, which achieve a near-optimal treewidth of O(log^2(n)). This result has significant implications for fixed-parameter tractability in graph minor theory and related fields such as graph planarity and minor-closed properties in treewidth. By leveraging our algorithm, we derive an optimization technique that enables solving various graph problems in treewidth in minor-based algorithms, resulting in parametric improvements in graph minor theory. This leads to novel and improved running times for treewidth representations and minor-based graph problems, surpassing previous bounds of O(n^(1/3)) and O(n^(1/2)).

For smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time systems that map R^n to R^n, with n greater than one, the long-term behavior of all non-trivial solutions under certain conditions can be described. It has been found that for a large class of such systems, the solutions either approach a fixed point or enter a periodic cycle of period two. This prevalent behavior can be traced back to specific instances of such systems, namely the Mackey-Glass equation and certain gradient systems associated with even potentials. Specific examples have been examined in more detail, providing insights into the prevalence of this behavior.

Quantum computers have the potential to solve extremely complex mathematical problems, 
specifically variational quantum (VQE) algorithms, across numerous fields of science.
Despite VQE's promise, there are inherent limitations to its current implementations.
This study presents an innovative approach called the Qubit-excitation adaptive VQE 
(QeAVQE), which surpasses VQE's constraints by leveraging a quantum-friendly 
H\'{o}rbach-L\'{o}wdin (HL) molecular orbital theory to construct an adaptive 
ansatz that rapidly models molecular orbitals at high levels of accuracy.
By utilizing QeAVQE, researchers can enhance electronic property calculations and 
improve reaction forecasting precision in chemistry, while also making progress in 
materials and reaction science. Experimental validation of QeAVQE is achievable on 
present quantum devices, potentially enabling efficient solving of intricate problems 
beyond quantum computers' capabilities until their full potential is realized in the 
future.

This research introduces a novel method for supervised representation learning, leveraging deep generative models to define a prior on latent space. A deep encoder is trained to fulfill this prior, and subsequently, representations estimated via maximum a posteriori (MAP) are found to possess favorable properties, including well-defined clustering, low dimensionality, and robustness to noise and adversarial inputs. As a result, these representations are suitable for constructing classifiers that can pinpoint areas of low-confidence to develop high-quality labeling datasets through human interaction. Furthermore, an extended application demonstrates that these representations estimated via MAP can also be utilized for semantic image tagging and image classification using a variational auto-encoder prior.

The growing discrepancy between the values of the deceleration parameter $q_0$ obtained from observations using cosmic distance moduli and supernovae data versus those using data from strong gravitational lensing and supernovae data has led to a notable tension between measured values. This tension, observed in 2022, has resulted in a value of $\sim1.9\sigma$ and may be a sign that our understanding of cosmic phenomena is incomplete. Furthermore, the value of $q_0$ obtained from NANOGrav's findings regarding continuous gravitational waves generated by supermassive binary black holes and stochastic gravitational waves has led to tension with measurements obtained from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Detector and the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observer for a period of $\sim10$ years. This tension, observed between NANOGrav's findings and those between the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Detector and the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observer, has resulted in a tension of $\sim2.0\sigma$. This may be a sign that our understanding of cosmic phenomena is incomplete. Furthermore, the Lambda-CDM model, which is our current best-fit model, fails to account for observations of $q_0$ and continuous gravitational waves. This tension, observed between NANOGrav's findings and those between the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Detector and the Laser Interfolometer Gr

A survey of carbon monosulfide in a comet, conducted using the Atacama Compact Array at a frequency of 3.129 GHz and a total of 33 GHz, revealed significant emission from a comet, catalogued as C/2015 ER61. The data showed a maximum signal of 10.8 sigma for CSM, indicating its presence within 1000 km of the comet's nucleus. An estimated production rate of 1.7 times 10^28 molecules per second was derived from the data, yielding a mass loss rate of 2.7 times 10^15 g per second. Our analysis suggests that CSM's production rate is consistent with water, indicating that it is likely produced by the sublimation of ice and not by the destruction of the comet's surface.

This research introduces a pioneering unsupervised approach to speech synthesis that does not require any initial knowledge of speech parameters. By leveraging pre-trained neural networks, the method can generate high-quality speech from an extensive amount of unlabelled audio data. It achieves this by calculating a speaker-specific encoding for each training example and using it to train a speech encoder and a normalizing flow model that can efficiently convert a standard, 1D sequence into a detailed, multi-dimensional representation tailored to the speaker's voice. As a result, our model can accurately synthesize speech from novel utterances and even adapt to significantly different speakers with minimal additional data. When compared to supervised alternatives, our unsupervised model produces nearly indistinguishable speech quality, as confirmed through both automated assessments and human evaluations. Furthermore, our model demonstrates exceptional computational efficiency, requiring only a fraction of the time to generate new utterances when compared to traditional, fully supervised models.

This study focuses on a specific variant of holographic dark energy, referred to as the Essence model, characterized by its variable equation of state. We have developed a comprehensive framework to examine the properties of this model, incorporating various factors, including the temperature of cosmic space based on the IR cutoff, and have derived an equation of state parameter with complex components. Our analysis reveals that the real component of this parameter can lead to successful resolution of the fine-tuning issue associated with cosmic dark energy, whereas its imaginary component indicates a variable phase of cosmic evolution, ultimately resulting in the transition from deceleration to acceleration.

Multi-objective Mixed-Integer Non Linear Optimization problems are ubiquitous in real-world applications and their solution methodologies are extensively reviewed in the literature, specifically focusing on evolutionary algorithms, which are explored to address this challenge.

We demonstrate that a smooth, connected Lie groupoid is internally stable along its path and a general Lie groupoid integral completes it within synthetic differential geometry. This is achieved through an alternative definition of connectivity, which is shown to be equivalent to a known result, allowing the identification of integrated paths with their corresponding integration objects. We provide a general theory for this purpose, establishing a relationship between Lie groupoids, their integrated paths, and their corresponding integration objects. This framework has implications in differential geometry within an axiomatic synthetic differential geometry context.

The amount of secure, high-quality, and well-documented medical image data available for training AI algorithms has surpassed the number of data points needed for successful machine learning. However, the challenge lies in organizing this data so that it can be easily accessed and trained on. This paper presents a framework to facilitate AI training by allowing data contributors to retain control and ensure security, as well as data users to access the data securely without compromising integrity. We demonstrate this approach through a framework utilizing Distributed Guest Accounts, Non-Repudiable Encryption, and the OWL 2 Reasoner to enable secure data sharing and AI training for biomedical data sharing cyberinfrastructure.

To improve aspect sentiment analysis, we developed a pre-trained model that efficiently captures emotion representations for aspects and their corresponding opinions, even when emotions and aspects are unrelated to one another. This understanding enables us to accurately detect the emotions in opinions relative to a given aspect. Consequently, we proposed the aSAP, a pre-training task that leverages these emotion representations through a contrastive learning approach. Furthermore, we modified the pre-training objective by incorporating a supervisory mask prediction task to enhance representation discrimination. Our model's pre-trained weights were then fine-tuned for aspect sentiment analysis and achieved superior results on six public benchmark datasets across multiple languages and styles of reviews, surpassing the current state-of-the-art performance by substantial margins.

We investigate identification and estimation strategies in tests of mediation, where case-control studies play a key role. These studies typically calculate odds ratios, which are considered proxies for causal effects, but current methods for estimating mediation effects in studies with binary outcomes often overlook the calculation of related probabilities, such as the conditional probability of a outcome given a treatment and a mediator. Our study aims to fill this knowledge gap by developing new identification and estimation methods for case-control studies with binary outcomes and middlemen, where conditions include sample randomness and binary classification models. Our results are illustrated through a study assessing risk factors for a disease, specifically how they influence an intermediate step, in this case, methylation levels.

This study tackles the challenge of designing robust beamformers for secure multiuser communication networks that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and suffer from hardware impairments.
We optimize the minimum achievable secrecy rate of multiuser networks subject to nonconvex constraints, including mobile user channel capacity and total transmit power.
To address these complexities, we partition the problem into two sub-problems and sequentially apply an alternating optimization approach, while also utilizing successive convex approximation.
Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm to solve the sub-problems and an external point method is used to handle the inexact solutions resulting from the approximation.
The proposed algorithm is verified through simulations, which also showcase its capability of achieving optimal power allocation when assuming perfect channel knowledge.

Our proposed approach to a fundamental issue in both artificial intelligence and human learning, known as the frame problem, involves selectively adjusting experiences derived from past actions. Rather than adjusting these experiences in real-time, our contrastive value strategy postulates that experiences are revisited and revised through a learning process after the fact. This theorethical model posits two key mechanisms: a) a learning agent reviews past actions in a reflective process, and b) adjusts its understanding of these actions by adopting a revised perspective. Our study aims to explore this theorethical model through a series of experiments to verify its effectiveness and provide a framework for understanding how learning agents can optimize their decisions in line with human values.

Investigations of solar breeze plasma and energetic particles in the inner heliosphere have been significantly enhanced by recent close-in observations made by Parker Solar Probe, which have now provided crucial insights into solar breeze energy flux. Energy flux measurements made by PSP's SWEAP instrument are particularly valuable for understanding the inner heliosphere, and early results from close-in observations are presented here. Data collected during six distinct PSP encounters, ranging in distance from 0.17 to 0.34 AU, are analyzed, revealing patterns in energy flux distribution. A notable increase in energy flux density with proximity to the Sun is observed, and findings indicate that solar breeze plasma and energetic particles dominate over background solar breeze plasma. A comparison with observations made by Helios missions and spacecraft such as ACE, SOHO, and STEREO reveals discrepancies, and it is suggested that these differences are a result of varying heliospheric distances and heliospheric conditions.

To establish a quantum version of a principal bundle, we develop a method of taking a free bundle G-space (X,π) and constructing a noncommutative version, namely the minimal cross-space [A(X)⊂G⊗A(X)]-bundle. This involves creating a new bundle based on a C*-algebra inclusion where G is amenable. Notably, for amenable groups, (G, 1) can be embedded in G⊗(G, 1) through our construction when (G, 1) is a free G-space. Furthermore, we show that a noncommutative space X* constructed from X and G retains key characteristics, such as K-theory, when applying our method to suspensions and reduced free products. These properties validate the construction as a true quantum analogue of principal bundles. Finally, we apply our construction to create matrix bundles on specific C*-algebras and characterize a class of noncommutative 3-manifolds that possess a principal SU(2)-bundle structure.

Research by Brendle and Miller in 1991 demonstrated that, in the context of the random model, a specific cardinal characteristic known as the ultrafilter number is less than another characteristic known as the almost disjointness number. We will present a different model of set theory in which another characteristic known as the nearly disjointness number is lower than the almost disjointness number, thereby implying that an inclusion previously assumed to be valid is not necessarily true.

This investigation focuses on investigating the clariification and chromatic enhancement effects in a $q$-deformed optomechanical system with a nonlinear oscillator described by an anharmonic oscillator potential deformed by Milne. We used an adiabatic-elimination approach to derive a maximally entangled Bell state between an optical mode and a mechanical mode deformed by Milne. We found that $q$-deformation can improve both the group velocity and the clarity effect. We observed that anti-TEMS can induce fast light and stable phase reconstruction, and that $q$-deformation can improve the clarity and fast light effects. We concluded that the standard optomechanical system can be outperformed by an optomechanical system with $q$-deformation.

Extending the Two-Rotors Model to incorporate R-parity, we found that incorporating negative R-parity states in nuclei like $^{184}$Os leads to a substantial increase in energy for the A1, A2, and B2 states, but significantly lowers the B1 state's energy, resulting in an adverse effect on the R-parity R-rotational band structure.  The key to this effect lies in a negative R-parity state that has an opposite orientation relative to the even-even parent nucleus, which, due to its high A factor, creates a large energy gap, especially impacting the B1 band.  The five-dimensional Hamiltonian including the Coriolis interaction provides a thorough explanation for these intriguing energy patterns.

A novel cell-mean based neural network method is developed to solve hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations in a concise abstract, utilizing a new neural network approximation for the left-biased spatial difference of a solution and another for the solution at the right boundary of a cell. This approach allows a PDE to be transformed into a set of ODEs or SDEs applicable in space, which are then solved using conventional ODE or MC methods for hyperbolic equations, and box schemes for a temporal discretization for parabolic equations. This method achieves a convergent and efficient solution with a detailed theoretical analysis and supporting numerical experiments for various equations.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC is focused on investigating the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and studying particle production mechanisms in various collision scenarios. The upcoming ALICE upgrade will significantly boost the experiment's capabilities in spatial and temporal resolutions, thereby enhancing its ability to detect hadrons and flow with superior precision. This paper will detail the current ALICE upgrade status and propose future enhancements aimed at expanding the experiment's reach beyond its primary objectives for LHC Run 3.

The Unruh effect describes how an accelerating detector perceives the Minkowski vacuum as a thermal state due to its motion. Our research shows that the past and future light cones of an accelerating detector are entangled even at zero temperature. By studying the past-future entanglement structure, we discovered a previously unknown timelike version of the Unruh phenomenon. In this new Unruh effect, the past-future entanglement reveals the detector's acceleration, and a geometric phase (Georgi phase) emerges from this entanglement. Our analysis hinges on the conventional Unruh effect and quantum field theory techniques. Additionally, the Gege phase can be understood through a time-based perspective of the acceleration, and it can be calculated by dividing the past-future entanglement into distinct Rindler wedges. A matrix product state (MPS) representation of the past-future entanglement is proposed to explain the geometric phase in a new, insightful way.

A significant challenge in disaster management is the effective extraction of critical incident information from social media posts, especially in multiple languages. This task is complicated by the diverse range of languages spoken and written by users globally, necessitating multilingual NLP models to process and analyze these posts during emergencies. Existing studies primarily focus on monolingual NLP for incident extraction, leaving a notable gap in multilingual incident extraction research. To address this gap, we introduce the Multilingual Emergency Incident Extraction (MEE) dataset, comprising over 15,000 real-world, noisily labeled social media posts from ten languages. Our findings reveal that current state-of-the-art NLP models, when directly applied to the MEE dataset, struggle to generalize well, highlighting the need for further investigation into multilingual NLP for real-world emergency management.

We derive new global characteristics under specific conditions on a map between
manifolds, leading to refined versions of Hartl's theorems on global
complexity and Xiang's theorems on global rank. Our theoretical framework
also provides insight into how the top Euler form behaves when a vector bundle
is modified through direct sum with its dual, building on Zhang's work.

Our analysis examines the impact of the stellar breeze on the correlation between hard X-ray intensity and pulse arrival time in Cyg X-1 during its hard state. Utilizing XMM-INT and XIS data, we discovered a substantial correlation between the breeze and XIS counts rates, both in time and in magnitude. Furthermore, we determined a minimal link between XIS and XINT pulses. This study revealed that the breeze contributes a substantial, yet unaccounted for, fraction of the modulated flux in the system. The findings indicate a substantial increase in the mass accretion rate modulation compared to previous models. Additionally, we observed a complex relationship between the breeze and various black hole mass and distance estimates, resulting in some implausible values. The study also revealed a minimal link between XIS and BZ light curves.

The study of a specific ether-like modification of general relativity, a specific
case of a broader theory, is a new area of research, with a focus on a thermally
modified Schwarzschild-like solution. Researchers have previously explored a
similar modification with an ether vector aligned with a uniform magnetic field,
resulting in a thermally modified black hole metric. Our analysis of this
modification with a magnetic field as a specific case of a more general
scenario reveals that the hole's temperature and entropy are influenced by the

Our approach to universal parsing simultaneously parses dependency trees, linguistic representations, and semantic representations, requiring no prior training or manual annotation.  The core of our model is a parser that uses both linguistic and semantic information to improve its overall performance.  By considering the dependency tree, linguistic representation, and semantic representation as interconnected, we've created a unified probabilistic framework that estimates the joint probability of all three.  The model's performance in terms of parsing accuracy has been tested and compared to systems that only focus on either dependency trees or linguistic representations as separate tasks, which require prior training data for the respective parsing types.

We utilize the magnetized, general-relativistic co-rotation column model to investigate the post-merger outflows generated by a range of scenarios involving nearly equal-sized stellar-mass black hole-neutron star mergers. We explore the impact of varying magnetic field strengths and co-rotation speeds on post-merger dynamics. Our results show that the co-rotation speed significantly influences post-merger outcomes, with faster rotation leading to larger and longer-lasting outflows due to increased magnetic field lines. Moreover, our calculations suggest that the average outflow speed, mass rate, and total mass are directly correlated with the strength of the magnetic field. We utilize these findings to establish relationships between these parameters and observable quantities such as the peak amplitude of gravitational wave signals, the mass ratio, and the spin of the neutron star. Our analysis reveals that the co-rotation speed has a substantial impact on the observed properties of post-merger outflows, with implications for electromagnetic observations of binary mergers.

Early-type galaxies in the local universe are believed to have been significantly influenced by tidal processes over their lifetimes. However, the substantial number of galaxies in these groups makes it a daunting task to assess the extent of tidal activity and its impact on their populations. We have made a crucial discovery by identifying galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program, a 10-year research project involving a deep sky survey. By utilizing a novel approach, we found that approximately 10-15% of early-type galaxies in the local universe exhibit tidal features, indicating that they were likely affected by tidal processes. This finding was observed for a sample of galaxies spanning a wide redshift range and out to a particular redshift threshold. We found that tidal features are more prevalent in galaxies with lower luminosities and those with higher concentrations of a galaxy's light in its core. Interestingly, our research revealed that tidal features are more prevalent in galaxies with lower concentrations of a galaxy's light in its core, suggesting that large galaxies may have experienced more major mergers than smaller ones.

A new azimuthally symmetric gravitational effect has been identified, expressed through a specific metric and field equations. This is a significant addition to our understanding of general relativity, providing an alternative explanation for bipolar stellar outflows without the need for accretion processes. The phenomenon is characterized by intense repulsive forces along the poles of a massive object, and the strength of this effect depends on the curvature of space, varying inversely with distance. Additionally, there is a specific mass threshold above which the outflow force surpasses the attractive gravitational pull, potentially allowing for the complete escape of particles at a specific latitude. A specific case involving a static point charge has also been explored, revealing how the outflow force interacts with electromagnetic forces. Finally, proposed solutions for this new effect include modifications to a stellar body's shape and density distribution.

We have conducted a detailed analysis of 11 Fast Radio Bursts observed by the CHIME/FRB telescope, specifically focusing on those with precisely measured arrival times and frequencies. By using data from the CHIME/FRB telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope, our research has placed the most restrictive constraints to date on the optical emission of the Crab pulsar and FRB 121102. The analysis has shown that the optical emission of the Crab pulsar is limited to specific intervals, while FRB 121102 has shown no detectable optical emission during and within 100 milliseconds after radio bursts, as well as between bursts. The limits have shown that the optical power of FRB 121102 is less than certain values, as well as placing strict bounds on the optical synchrotron emission of FRB 121102. High-power laser systems are designed using advanced computational techniques, 
specifically to model complex interactions between light and matter that are 
difficult to solve analytically or through simple model assumptions. By employing 
realistic designs, researchers can enhance laser performance by optimizing the 
distribution of materials, which in turn can lead to significant improvements in 
target illumination. Furthermore, the use of machine learning and reverse engineering 
methods enables the identification of optimal target configurations, which, when 
combined with existing design models, can unlock new insights and capabilities. This 
approach has been successfully implemented in various high-power laser systems, such 
as Omega and NIF, paving the way for innovative applications and fundamental model 
improvements.

Current language models are highly skilled at understanding and processing written text, but when it comes to visual elements, they're limited to pre-existing descriptions. Our study explores how large-scale language models can be adapted to incorporate visual control, like images and layouts, by incorporating tools like HLSVH-1, a visual highlighting language, and-kivy for GUI generation. Our approach involves fine-tuning existing language models, like GPT-J, on a large dataset of paired text and code, called HUGO, to simultaneously learn text, visual observation, and code generation. The results show our model can produce accurate and functional user interfaces that match paired text descriptions, as well as more complex complex ones that were not part of the training data, demonstrating its ability to integrate multiple levels of visual control, including default settings.
